lead: A thyristor is a latch: once anode current exceeds the latching value, the gate loses control. Turn-on needs a small local trigger to start that latch. Gate triggering is the usual method because it is fast and controllable. A gate circuit must deliver a steep pulse with enough voltage and current at the gate-cathode terminals, then remove the pulse after latching. The same idea appears in a dimmer, a battery charger and an HVDC valve.
prereq: You need: the PNPN structure, the two-transistor model and latching current from Chapter 1.2.

sections.h3: Five ways a thyristor turns on

blocks.text: An SCR in forward blocking has two stable states: off and on. Five physical actions can move it to on.

items: Gate: a positive current into the gate-cathode junction injects carriers. The two internal transistors regenerate and the SCR latches. This is the normal controlled method.
Thermal: high junction temperature raises leakage current. At a critical temperature the leakage alone can trigger the device. This is unwanted turn-on; heat sinks and thermal design prevent it.

Light: photons absorbed near a junction create electron-hole pairs. A light-triggered thyristor has a small optical gate; it is used in high-voltage HVDC valves because it isolates control from the high-voltage side.

Forward-voltage breakover: if anode voltage reaches the forward breakover voltage V<sub>BO</sub>, avalanche multiplication triggers the SCR. This stresses the device and is not a normal control method.
dv/dt: a fast rise of anode voltage charges the junction capacitance. The displacement current C dv/dt acts like gate current and can false-trigger the SCR. See Chapter 1.7 for snubbers.

blocks.text: Gate turn-on is preferred because the designer chooses the instant; the other four are either slow, destructive or accidental.

The gate-cathode path is a PN junction, so its V-I curve is like a diode: current rises sharply after a knee. Two datasheet numbers define triggering. V<sub>GT</sub> is the gate-cathode voltage that turns on every device of that type at a stated temperature and anode voltage. I<sub>GT</sub> is the corresponding gate current. They are minimum values for reliable turn-on, not maximum ratings.

The series resistor sets the gate current. If a trigger source V<sub>s</sub> drives the gate through R<sub>s</sub>, then R<sub>s</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>GT</sub>) / I<sub>GT</sub>. The resistor must carry the pulse current; its peak power is I<sub>GT</sub>² R<sub>s</sub> and its average power is lower by the duty ratio.

Pulse shape matters. A gate pulse should rise quickly, often below 1 µs, and stay on long enough for anode current to exceed the latching current I<sub>L</sub>. Typical pulse widths are 10 µs to 50 µs. A long DC gate current wastes power and can heat the gate. The pulse is removed after latching; holding current is the lower current at which an already-on SCR turns off.

sections.h3: Trigger circuits: R, RC, UJT and pulse transformer

blocks.text: Four gate trigger circuits appear in exams.

items: R triggering: a resistor from a DC supply to the gate. It is simple and cheap. It applies continuous gate current, wastes power and gives no isolation. Use it only in low-cost small SCR circuits.

RC triggering: a capacitor charges through a resistor; when the control switch closes, the capacitor discharges into the gate through a resistor. The capacitor gives a short pulse and can also shift phase in AC controllers.

UJT relaxation oscillator: a UJT has an emitter and two bases. With base supply V<sub>BB</sub>, the emitter peak voltage is V<sub>P</sub> = η V<sub>BB</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>, where η is the intrinsic standoff ratio and V<sub>D</sub> is a diode drop. The capacitor charges through R until V<sub>P</sub>; the UJT fires, discharges the capacitor, and a voltage pulse across base-1 resistor R1 triggers the SCR. Some syllabi call this a relaxation oscillator.

Pulse transformer: a small transformer couples the control pulse to the gate. It isolates the control circuit from the power circuit and can invert polarity. The core cannot pass a long DC pulse, so the pulse width is limited; use a short pulse or a pulse train.

spec.title: Gate trigger path
spec.aria: A control pulse and a 12 V source feed a 105 Ω series resistor, which drives the SCR gate-cathode path.

examples.question: A 12 V trigger source drives an SCR gate. The datasheet gives V_GT = 1.5 V and I_GT = 100 mA. Find the series gate resistance R_s and the peak power lost in it when the gate pulse is on.
steps: Convert the gate current: I_GT = 100 mA = 0.100 A.
Voltage across the series resistor: V_s − V_GT = 12 V − 1.5 V = 10.5 V.
Peak pulse power in R_s: P = I_GT² R_s = (0.100 A)² × 105 Ω = 1.05 W.
examples.answer: The series gate resistance is 105 Ω and its peak pulse power is 1.05 W.
examples.check:
Vs = 12.0
Vgt = 1.5
Igt = 0.100
Rs = (Vs - Vgt) / Igt
P = Igt**2 * Rs
print(Rs)
print(P)

traps: V_GT and I_GT are minimum trigger values, not absolute maxima. Driving exactly at these values may fail at low temperature; use a margin.
The gate resistor sees peak pulse power I²R, not average DC power. A 1.05 W pulse in a 0.25 W resistor can still fail if the pulse is long or repeated fast.
Latching current and holding current are different. Latching is the anode current needed to keep the SCR on when the gate is removed; holding is the lower current at which an on SCR turns off.
dv/dt turn-on is not caused by gate current. It is junction-capacitance displacement current; a snubber or softer anode voltage slows dv/dt.
A pulse transformer blocks DC. A single long gate pulse saturates it; use a short pulse or a pulse train.

quiz.q: List the five ways an SCR can turn on.
quiz.a: Gate current, thermal leakage, light, forward-voltage breakover, and dv/dt displacement current.
V_GT is the gate-cathode voltage that reliably turns on every device of a type at stated conditions. I_GT is the corresponding gate current.

quiz.q: Why is the gate pulse removed after latching?
quiz.a: After anode current exceeds latching current, the internal transistors regenerate without gate current. Keeping the gate pulse on wastes power and heats the gate.

quiz.q: How does a UJT relaxation oscillator generate a gate pulse?
quiz.a: A capacitor charges until the UJT emitter reaches V_P = ηV_BB + V_D. The UJT then fires and discharges the capacitor through base-1, producing a voltage pulse across R1 that triggers the SCR.

quiz.q: A 15 V source triggers an SCR with V_GT = 1.2 V and I_GT = 50 mA. Find R_s and the peak pulse power in it.
A circuit false-triggers when an adjacent contactor opens. Explain the likely cause and one fix.
quiz.a: The contactor creates a fast anode-voltage rise; junction capacitance passes displacement current C dv/dt that acts like gate current. Add an RC snubber or slow the anode voltage rise, and keep gate wiring short and shielded.

quiz.q: Why is simple R triggering poor for a mains-fed SCR?
quiz.a: It applies continuous gate current, wasting power and heating the gate. It gives no isolation from the mains and cannot produce a clean short pulse; it is limited to small low-cost circuits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial gate drives use integrated drivers with isolated supplies and fault protection; for very high voltage, light-triggered thyristors remove the gate transformer. Digital isolators and fibre optics carry trigger pulses across high-voltage barriers. Wide-band-gap devices need faster, more precise gate pulses, so gate-loop inductance becomes a design issue. Search for 'SCR gate drive circuit', 'light-triggered thyristor' and 'isolated gate driver'.
